Reading lists

3,088 readings from 33 PhD syllabi and reading lists in organization theory and strategy, merged and regrouped by theoretical stream. The number beside each reading is how many of the 33 syllabi assign it. Each stream opens with its core readings, the 123 that appear in 4 or more syllabi, followed by those assigned in two or three; readings that appear in only one syllabus are folded away at the end. Credit for the selections belongs to the instructors listed at the end of the page.

Theory tree

Each box is a stream, with its number of readings; click a box to jump to its list. Arrows show which streams grew out of which; hover over an arrow for a one-line explanation. Outside the tree: Theory and theorizing (55), Social theory (85), Research methods (187) and The academic profession (66).

Lineage, in words
  • Classical foundations → Contingency and configurational theory. Open-systems thinking turned attention to fit with the environment.
  • Classical foundations → Culture, cognition and sensemaking. Weber and Durkheim on meaning and legitimate order.
  • Classical foundations → Behavioral theory of the firm and organizational learning. Barnard and Simon on bounded rationality in administration.
  • Classical foundations → Organizational economics. Coase asked why firms exist at all.
  • Contingency and configurational theory → Resource dependence and power. From adapting to the environment to managing dependence on it.
  • Contingency and configurational theory → Organizational ecology and demography. From adaptation to selection by the environment.
  • Organizational ecology and demography → Entrepreneurship and new organizations. Founding rates and the liability of newness.
  • Organizational ecology and demography → Categories, identity and authenticity. Organizational forms as socially coded identities.
  • Culture, cognition and sensemaking → Institutional theory. Taken-for-granted meaning becomes structure.
  • Institutional theory → Categories, identity and authenticity. Classification and identity as institutional processes.
  • Institutional theory → Social movements, power and inequality. Contesting and changing institutions.
  • Social networks and embeddedness → Status and social evaluation. Ties as prisms that signal quality.
  • Status and social evaluation → Categories, identity and authenticity. Audiences evaluate actors through categories.
  • Social movements, power and inequality → Nonmarket strategy and corporate social responsibility. Firms respond to activists, publics and the state.
  • Behavioral theory of the firm and organizational learning → Evolutionary theory, technology and innovation. Routines and search, scaled up to industries.
  • Behavioral theory of the firm and organizational learning → Strategy process, practice and cognition. Attention and decision making in strategy.
  • Evolutionary theory, technology and innovation → Resource-based view and capabilities. Capabilities and dynamic capabilities.
  • Economic perspectives on strategy → Resource-based view and capabilities. From industry position to firm-specific resources.
  • Organizational economics → Corporate strategy and interfirm relationships. Make-or-buy, alliances and the scope of the firm.
  • Organizational economics → Corporate governance and upper echelons. Agency problems between owners and managers.
  • Organizational economics → International business and multinationals. Internalization theory of the multinational.

Resource dependence and power

Interdependence, power and how organizations manage their environments.

Drawn from: Pollock (University of Tennessee, Knoxville); Sullivan (HKUST); Dobbin (Harvard); Marquis (Harvard); Wan (CUHK); Yiu (CUHK); Lu, Li, Park, Yang & Yan (CityU); Fiss (USC); Lounsbury (); Clough (UBC); Anteby (Boston University); Zuckerman (MIT Sloan School of Management); Yue (USC); Peng (UT Dallas); Maoret (IESE); Amit (Wharton).

Social networks and embeddedness

Embeddedness, weak ties, structural holes, brokerage and interorganizational networks.

Drawn from: Martin (University of California at Berkeley); Maoret (IESE); Zuckerman (MIT Sloan School of Management); Pollock (University of Tennessee, Knoxville); Chandrasekhar (Stanford University); Clough (UBC); Yue (USC); Marquis (Harvard); Sullivan (HKUST); Dobbin (Harvard); Lu, Li, Park, Yang & Yan (CityU); DiMaggio (Princeton University); Fiss (USC); McDonnell (Wharton); Peng (UT Dallas); Anteby (Boston University); DiMaggio (Princeton University); Levinthal (Wharton); Wan (CUHK); Zhou (HKU); Amit (Wharton); Yiu (CUHK); Lounsbury (); Jia (USC); Yao (Harvard).

Culture, cognition and sensemaking

Culture, sensemaking, framing and symbolic management.

Drawn from: DiMaggio (Princeton University); Maoret (IESE); Pollock (University of Tennessee, Knoxville); Glaser (Alberta); DiMaggio (Princeton University); Lounsbury (); Anteby (Boston University); Jia (USC); Fiss (USC); Martin (University of California at Berkeley); Yue (USC); Clough (UBC); Cameron (Wharton); Keum (Columbia Business School); Sullivan (HKUST); Zuckerman (MIT Sloan School of Management); McDonnell (Wharton); Amit (Wharton); Zhou (HKU); Yiu (CUHK); Peng (UT Dallas).

Drawn from: Jia (USC); Pollock (University of Tennessee, Knoxville); Levinthal (Wharton); Sullivan (HKUST); Maoret (IESE); Yiu (CUHK); Wan (CUHK); Keum (Columbia Business School); Fiss (USC); Clough (UBC); Yao (Harvard); Peng (UT Dallas); Zhou (HKU); Anteby (Boston University); Glaser (Alberta); Dobbin (Harvard); Zuckerman (MIT Sloan School of Management).
